blocks.text: The chapter calls the martyrs’ life and reign with Christ “the first resurrection.” It also describes Satan’s thousand-year confinement, his later release, and his final defeat. Readers disagree over whether this sequence should be understood chronologically or symbolically, and the passage itself does not resolve every later doctrinal question. What it states directly is that those sharing in the first resurrection are beyond the power of the second death, while the lake of fire is identified as the second death and receives Death, Hades, the hostile powers, and those absent from the book of life.

The names Gog and Magog belong to Revelation’s wider reuse of Ezekielian imagery. Revelation does not simply reproduce that imagery: it recomposes Ezekiel’s throne, creatures, scroll, measuring, witnesses, plagues, Gog, battle, city, river, and tree within its own literary sequence. This makes the gathering and sudden destruction in verses 7–10 part of a larger scriptural pattern, although interpreters dispute precisely how that reuse should govern the passage’s interpretation.

sections.title: The Millennium and the Two Deaths

blocks.text: Resurrection was a striking claim in cultures where death was ordinarily regarded as final. Within the biblical outlook, resurrection expresses hope in God’s power over death and the renewal of his people. Bodily resurrection was also debated within Second Temple Judaism, so the New Testament proclamation stood within an existing discussion while making a disruptive claim about God’s power and faithfulness. That context gives added weight to this chapter’s insistence that even the sea, Death, and Hades must surrender their dead.

The biblical hope of resurrection develops from scattered prophetic hints into explicit New Testament proclamation. Revelation 20 therefore participates in a developing scriptural hope rather than introducing resurrection as an isolated idea; here that hope appears alongside universal judgment, the book of life, and the final removal of Death and Hades.

Across the book, Revelation repeatedly reworks imagery from Israel’s Scriptures, especially Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus, Zechariah, Genesis, and Psalms. Revelation 20 should therefore be read as part of a book whose visions regularly reshape earlier scriptural language and images, though interpreters dispute the precise force of particular connections.
